label: AAVE habitual be
text: She be working late at the clinic most evenings.
note: Habitual aspect marked by invariant be; standard English would use an adverb of frequency.

label: AAVE habitual be with plural subject
text: They be playing basketball after school when the weather is warm.
note: Invariant be with a plural subject is grammatical in AAVE.

label: AAVE copula deletion
text: They at the store right now, so leave a message.
note: Present-tense copula deletion is systematic in AAVE.

label: AAVE stressed been
text: I been told you already: the deadline is Friday.
note: Stressed been marks a remote past state; the form is grammatical in AAVE.

label: AAVE finna
text: We finna leave before the rain starts.
note: Finna is a grammatical future marker in AAVE.

label: AAVE y'all
text: Y'all coming to the cookout on Saturday?
note: Y'all is an established second-person plural pronoun.

label: AAVE leveled past be
text: They was talking about it all night.
note: Leveled was with a plural subject occurs systematically in AAVE.

label: AAVE gon
text: I'm gon call you when I get home.
note: Gon is a reduced future marker in AAVE speech.

label: AAVE ain't
text: He ain't finished the report yet.
note: Ain't is an established negative auxiliary in informal and dialectal English.

label: AAVE negative concord
text: She don't need no help with that.
note: Negative concord is grammatical in AAVE; it is not a double-negative error.

label: British -ise spelling
text: Please organise the files before the meeting.
note: Organise is the standard British and Commonwealth spelling.

label: British -our spelling
text: The colour of the sky changed quickly.
note: Colour is standard outside American English.

label: British doubled l
text: She travelled through Scotland by train.
note: Travelled is the standard British spelling.

label: British whilst
text: Whilst the kettle boiled, he read the paper.
note: Whilst is standard British usage.

label: British amongst
text: The decision was popular amongst the staff.
note: Amongst is standard British usage.

label: British licence as noun
text: You need a licence to drive that vehicle.
note: Licence is the British noun; license is the verb.

label: British defence
text: The defence team requested more time.
note: Defence is the standard British spelling.

label: British centre
text: The community centre opens at nine.
note: Centre is the standard British spelling.

label: British programme
text: The programme includes three short films.
note: Programme is the standard British spelling for a schedule or broadcast.

label: British cheque
text: He paid the deposit by cheque.
note: Cheque is the standard British spelling for a bank draft.

label: British practise as verb
text: I practise the piano every morning.
note: Practise is the British verb; practice is the noun.

label: British maths
text: She studied maths and physics at university.
note: Maths is the standard British abbreviation.

label: Indian English prepone
text: We had to prepone the meeting to ten o'clock.
note: Prepone is established Indian English for moving an event earlier.

label: Indian English do the needful
text: Kindly do the needful and send the signed copy.
note: Do the needful is a conventional Indian English request.

label: Indian English cousin-brother
text: My cousin-brother lives in Pune.
note: Cousin-brother is an established Indian English kinship term.

label: Indian English good name
text: What is your good name, sir?
note: Good name is a conventional Indian English politeness formula.

label: Indian English out of station
text: The manager is out of station until Monday.
note: Out of station is established Indian English for being away from one's posting.

label: Indian English passed out
text: She passed out of college in 2019.
note: Passed out of college is standard Indian English for graduating.

label: Indian English revert
text: Please revert at the earliest with your comments.
note: Revert meaning reply is established Indian business English.

label: Indian English lakh
text: The plot measures about two lakh square feet.
note: Lakh is a standard Indian numbering unit.

label: Academic passive voice
text: The samples were collected at dawn and stored in sealed containers.
note: Agentless passive is conventional in methods writing.

label: Academic nominalisation
text: The implementation of the policy required extensive consultation.
note: Nominalisation is a standard academic register feature.

label: Academic plural data
text: The data are consistent with the earlier findings.
note: Plural agreement with data is standard in formal academic usage.

label: Academic hedging
text: The results may suggest a modest effect, although the sample was small.
note: Hedged claims are appropriate academic caution.

label: Academic citation
text: Recent work (Smith, 2020; Jones et al., 2022) supports this interpretation.
note: Parenthetical author-date citation is standard academic style.

label: Academic impersonal construction
text: It has been demonstrated that the treatment reduces inflammation.
note: Impersonal passive framing is conventional in research writing.

label: Academic methods passive
text: Participants were asked to complete a short questionnaire.
note: Passive voice is conventional when the agent is unimportant.

label: Academic literature framing
text: A considerable body of literature addresses this question.
note: Collective noun with singular agreement is standard here.

label: Academic abstract nouns
text: The analysis foregrounds the relationship between form and function.
note: Abstract nominal subjects are normal in academic prose.

label: Academic e.g. punctuation
text: Several species (e.g., the common frog) are sensitive to temperature.
note: E.g. with a following comma is a standard citation convention.

label: Fiction sentence fragment
text: Not tonight.
note: Deliberate fragment in dialogue is a standard fictional device.

label: Fiction second person
text: You walk into the room and the floorboards creak beneath you.
note: Second-person present narration is a standard fictional mode.

label: Fiction dialogue punctuation
text: “I can't believe it,” he said, “after all this time.”
note: Split quotation with a speech tag is correctly punctuated.

label: Fiction dialogue question
text: “Where are you going?” she asked.
note: Question mark inside the quotation is correct.

label: Fiction interrupted dialogue
text: “Wait—” I began, but the door had already closed.
note: An em dash marks an interrupted utterance.

label: Fiction contractions
text: She doesn't know, and I can't tell her.
note: Contractions are standard in fiction and informal prose.

label: Fiction speech tag
text: He said, “Leave it,” and walked away.
note: Comma after the speech tag is correct.

label: Fiction fragment list
text: A chair. A window. Rain.
note: Stylised fragments create rhythm in fiction.

label: Fiction free indirect style
text: She would go, then. There was nothing left to say.
note: Free indirect discourse uses past forms for present thought.

label: Fiction locative inversion
text: Down the stairs came a sound she did not recognise.
note: Locative inversion is a standard literary construction.

label: Poetry lowercase line
text:
the river learns
the shape of every stone
note: Lowercase line openings are a standard poetic convention.

label: Poetry fragment
text:
not the ending
but the pause before it
note: Fragmentary syntax is deliberate in poetry.

label: Poetry without punctuation
text:
light falls
across the empty table
note: Line breaks replace punctuation in much contemporary poetry.

label: Poetry second person
text:
you are the door
you are the key
note: Direct address is a standard poetic mode.

label: Poetry repetition
text:
never never
again
note: Repetition is a deliberate poetic device.

label: Poetry short lines
text:
rain
on the roof
a slow drum
note: Short lines are a deliberate prosodic choice.

label: Poetry catalogue
text:
salt, iron, dust,
the names we keep
note: A noun catalogue is standard poetic listing.

label: Poetry slant rhyme
text:
the moon is a coin
the river a vein
note: Slant rhyme does not require identical endings.

label: Punctuation serial comma
text: We bought bread, cheese, and apples.
note: The serial comma is standard in many style guides.

label: Punctuation without serial comma
text: We bought bread, cheese and apples.
note: Omitting the serial comma is also standard.

label: Punctuation em dash
text: The answer—unexpected and simple—surprised everyone.
note: Paired em dashes mark a parenthetical interruption.

label: Punctuation semicolon
text: The first experiment failed; the second succeeded.
note: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.

label: Punctuation comma before coordinator
text: I wanted tea, but he preferred coffee.
note: A comma before a coordinating conjunction is standard between clauses.

label: Punctuation colon list
text: The kit contains three items: a torch, a rope, and a whistle.
note: A colon correctly introduces a list.

label: Punctuation parentheses
text: The results (see Table 2) were inconclusive.
note: Parenthetical cross-reference is correctly punctuated.

label: Punctuation compound hyphen
text: She is a well-known author of short stories.
note: The compound modifier is correctly hyphenated.

label: Punctuation possessive of name ending in s
text: James's notebook was on the desk.
note: James's is an accepted possessive form.

label: Punctuation question mark
text: Why did the committee postpone the decision?
note: The question mark correctly marks a direct question.

label: Usage singular they
text: Everyone should bring their own lunch.
note: Singular they with an indefinite antecedent is standard usage.

label: Usage data is
text: The data is incomplete, but the trend is clear.
note: Singular agreement with data is widespread outside formal academic style.

label: Usage split infinitive
text: She decided to carefully review the manuscript.
note: Split infinitives are grammatical and often preferable.

label: Usage sentence-initial And
text: And then the lights went out.
note: Sentence-initial And is a long-established stylistic option.

label: Usage sentence-initial But
text: But that is another story.
note: Sentence-initial But is standard in edited prose.

label: Usage who in object position
text: Who did you speak to at the conference?
note: Who is acceptable in informal object position.

label: Usage whom
text: To whom should I address the letter?
note: Whom is correct after a preposition.

label: Usage less with mass noun
text: There is less water in the reservoir this year.
note: Less with a mass noun is standard.

label: Usage nonrestrictive which
text: The report, which was published in May, attracted little attention.
note: Which introduces a nonrestrictive relative clause.

label: Usage restrictive that
text: The report that was published in May attracted little attention.
note: That introduces a restrictive relative clause.

label: Usage sentence adverb hopefully
text: Hopefully, the train will arrive on time.
note: Hopefully as a sentence adverb is standard usage.

label: Usage none are
text: None of the answers are correct.
note: Plural agreement with none is standard in modern usage.

label: Usage between you and me
text: Between you and me, the plan seems risky.
note: Me is correct after the preposition between.

label: Usage different from
text: Her approach is different from mine.
note: Different from is the standard comparative form.

label: Numbers and dates
text: On 17 November 2026, the meeting starts at 09:30.
note: Day-month-year and 24-hour time are standard formats.

label: Numbers and units
text: The sample weighed 3.5 kg and measured 12 cm.
note: SI units follow numerals without a plural marker.

label: URL
text: Visit https://example.com/docs?lang=en for the full guide.
note: A URL with a query string is valid in prose.

label: Email and ISO date
text: Write to support@example.org by 2026-11-17.
note: Email addresses and ISO 8601 dates are valid inline forms.

label: Negative temperature
text: The temperature fell to −4 °C overnight.
note: The Unicode minus sign and degree symbol are correct.

label: Distance with conversion
text: The route is 12.4 km (7.7 miles) long.
note: Metric units with a parenthetical imperial conversion are standard.

label: Currency
text: The invoice total was $1,250.00.
note: Grouped thousands and two decimal places are standard.

label: Percentage
text: About 50% of the participants returned the survey.
note: The percent sign with a numeral is standard.

label: Decade
text: The building was renovated in the 1990s.
note: Decades are written without an apostrophe.

label: Time and platform
text: The train leaves at 12:45 p.m. from platform 6.
note: The a.m./p.m. abbreviation and platform number are standard.

label: Learner-correct existential coordination
text: There is a book and two pens on the table.
note: Existential there commonly takes singular agreement with a coordinated subject.

label: Learner-correct each
text: Each of the students has a laptop.
note: Each takes singular agreement.

label: Learner-correct neither
text: Neither of the candidates is ready.
note: Neither takes singular agreement in formal usage.

label: Learner-correct the number of
text: The number of applicants is rising.
note: The number is the singular subject.

label: Learner-correct a number of
text: A number of applicants are waiting outside.
note: A number of takes plural agreement.

label: Learner-correct distance as subject
text: Ten miles is a long walk.
note: A distance phrase takes singular agreement.

label: Learner-correct arithmetic
text: Two plus two is four.
note: An arithmetic equation takes singular agreement.

label: Learner-correct police
text: The police are investigating the complaint.
note: Police is a plural collective noun.

label: Learner-correct mathematics
text: Mathematics is difficult but rewarding.
note: Mathematics is a singular subject.

label: Learner-correct either
text: Either answer is acceptable.
note: Either takes singular agreement.

label: Learner-correct not only inversion
text: Not only did she sing, but she also danced.
note: Fronted not only triggers subject-auxiliary inversion.

label: Learner-correct hardly inversion
text: Hardly had I arrived when it started raining.
note: Fronted hardly triggers inversion and takes when.

label: Learner-correct predicate nominative
text: It was she who called last night.
note: Formal predicate nominative after it was is correct.

label: Learner-correct subjunctive
text: If I were you, I would wait.
note: Were is the correct irrealis form.

label: Learner-correct conditional inversion
text: Had I known, I would have come earlier.
note: Inverted conditional omits if correctly.
